## What is LaTeX, and why Overleaf?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.nonincremental}
- **LaTeX** is plain text with markup, *compiled* into a PDF.
- You write what you *mean*; LaTeX does the layout.
- **Physicists use it** for equations, numbering, cross-references, and bibliographies.
- **Overleaf** is LaTeX in your browser. Free with your GT email; nothing to install.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {style="font-size: 1.25em;"}
```latex
\section{Newton's second law}
The net force is $F = ma$, so
\begin{equation}
  a = \frac{F}{m}.
\end{equation}
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; border: 1px solid #B3A369; padding: 0.4em 0.9em;"}
**1&nbsp;&nbsp;Newton's second law**

The net force is $F = ma$, so
$$a = \frac{F}{m}. \tag{1}$$
:::
:::
::::

::: {.cite-note}
Source: [@latexproject; @overleaf_learn30]
:::

::: notes
The right column is source on top and output below. Point out that the section number and the
equation number were not typed; LaTeX assigned them. Contrast with Word: what you see is what you
get, versus what you mean is what you get. Journals (APS, arXiv), theses, and many grant proposals
expect LaTeX. Overleaf also gives shared editing, version history, and templates (lab reports, CVs,
theses). A local install (TeX Live or MiKTeX plus an
editor) is an option later, but Overleaf is all they need for this course. Check before class that
signing up with a GT email still links to Georgia Tech's institutional Overleaf account.
:::

## Anatomy of a LaTeX document

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
```latex
\documentclass[12pt, letterpaper]{article}
\usepackage{amsmath}   % better math
\usepackage{graphicx}  % images
\title{PHYS 2211, HW 5, Problem 3}
\author{Your Name}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\section{Problem Statement}
A ball is launched at speed $v_0$ and
angle $\theta$ above level ground.
Find its \textbf{range} $R$.
\end{document}
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.nonincremental}
- **Preamble:** class, packages, title.
- **Body:** what appears on the page.
- Commands start with `\`.
- `{}` holds arguments; `[]` holds options.
- Environments: `\begin` &hellip; `\end`.
- `%` starts a comment.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.cite-note}
Source: [@oetiker2021]
:::

::: notes
The preamble is everything before \begin{document}. Blank lines separate paragraphs; extra spaces
and single line breaks are ignored. LaTeX ignores everything after a % on that line.
:::

## Live demo: building a homework note

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.nonincremental}
1. **New Project &rarr; Blank Project**
2. Title, author, `\maketitle`
3. Three `\section`s
4. A list: `itemize`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.nonincremental}
5. Equations: `\label`, `\eqref`
6. A figure with a `\caption`
7. Break it; read the error
8. **Download** PDF and source
:::
:::
::::

::: {.highlight-box}
Open [Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com/) and follow along. By the end, you will have a starting point for the [Homework in LaTeX](../assignments/deliverables/latex-homework.qmd) assignment.
:::

::: {.cite-note}
Source: [@overleaf_learn30; @overleaf_images]
:::

::: notes
Before class: build the finished demo project once, download it as a zip, and keep a PDF of it in
case the Wi-Fi or Overleaf is down. Have a photo of a hand-drawn trajectory sketch ready to upload
(trajectory.png).

Worked problem (PHYS 2211 style): a ball is launched from level ground with speed v0 at angle
theta. Find its range R.

Step 4, list of given quantities:

```latex
\begin{itemize}
  \item $v_0$: launch speed (m/s)
  \item $\theta$: launch angle above the horizontal
  \item $g = 9.8~\text{m/s}^2$: gravitational acceleration
\end{itemize}
```

Step 5, the equation and a reference back to it:

```latex
The ball lands when $y = 0$, at $t = 2 v_0 \sin\theta / g$.
Multiplying by the horizontal speed $v_0 \cos\theta$ gives
\begin{equation}
  R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}.
  \label{eq:range}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{eq:range} is largest at $\theta = 45^\circ$.
```

Step 6, the figure:

```latex
\begin{figure}[h]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{trajectory.png}
  \caption{Trajectory of the ball.}
  \label{fig:traj}
\end{figure}
```

Step 7, three breaks: (1) type "100% of the time" in a sentence; there is no error, the rest of the
line silently disappears. Fix with a backslash before the percent sign. (2) Type v_0 outside math
and show "Missing \$ inserted." (3) Delete a closing brace and show how the log points to the line.

Interpretation section (say it, maybe type it): units are (m/s)^2 / (m/s^2) = m; R = 0 at theta = 0
and at 90 degrees; v0 = 10 m/s at 45 degrees gives about 10.2 m, which is reasonable for a thrown
ball.
:::

## Writing math

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| `x^2`, `v_0`, `x_{\max}` | $x^2$, $v_0$, $x_{\max}$ |
| `\frac{a}{b}`, `\sqrt{2gh}` | $\frac{a}{b}$, $\sqrt{2gh}$ |
| `\theta`, `\omega`, `\Delta E` | $\theta$, $\omega$, $\Delta E$ |
| `\vec{F}`, `\hat{x}` | $\vec{F}$, $\hat{x}$ |
| `\int_0^T v\,dt` | $\int_0^T v\,dt$ |
| `\approx`, `\pm`, `\times` | $\approx$, $\pm$, $\times$ |
| `9.8~\text{m/s}^2` | $9.8~\text{m/s}^2$ |
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Inline**, inside a sentence: `$...$`

**Displayed and numbered:**

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
```latex
\begin{equation}
  R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}
  \label{eq:range}
\end{equation}
```
:::

**Refer back:** `Eq.~\eqref{eq:range}` gives "Eq. (1)", and the number updates itself.
:::
::::

::: {.highlight-box}
Use `equation*` or `\[...\]` for unnumbered equations.
:::

::: {.cite-note}
Source: [@overleaf_math] &middot; Can't find a symbol? Draw it in Detexify [@detexify].
:::

::: notes
\eqref, equation*, and \text all need \usepackage{amsmath}. Detexify lets you draw a symbol and
gives you the command.
:::

## When it won't compile

| Message | Usual cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Undefined control sequence` | Typo in a command, or a missing package | Check spelling; add the `\usepackage` |
| `Missing $ inserted` | `^`, `_`, or Greek outside math | Wrap it in `$...$` |
| `Runaway argument` | A `{` with no matching `}` | Find and close the brace |
| Text vanishes after `%` | `%` starts a comment | Write `\%` (also `\&`, `\$`, `\#`, `\_`) |
| `File not found` | Image not uploaded, or the name differs | Match the file name exactly |

::: {.highlight-box}
**Recompile often.** Fix the **first** error first; the log gives you the line number.
:::

::: notes
Overleaf's log panel links each error to its line in the editor. Errors often cascade: one missing
brace can produce ten messages, and fixing the first one clears the rest.
:::

## Writing up a solution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.nonincremental}
- Write for a reader who has not seen the assignment.
- Define every symbol the first time it appears, with units.
- Put words between equations. Equations are part of sentences and take punctuation.
- Check your answer, units, size, and limiting cases.
- Give every figure a **caption** and refer to it in text.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; border: 1px solid #B3A369; padding: 0.4em 0.9em;"}
**Less effective**

$y = v_0 \sin\theta \, t - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2 = 0$<br>
$t = 2 v_0 \sin\theta / g$<br>
$R = v_0^2 \sin 2\theta / g$
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; border: 1px solid #B3A369; padding: 0.4em 0.9em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
**More effective**

The ball lands when its height returns to zero, $v_0 \sin\theta \, t - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2 = 0$, so its flight time is $t = 2 v_0 \sin\theta / g$. Multiplying by its horizontal speed $v_0 \cos\theta$ gives the range
$$R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}. \tag{1}$$
At $\theta = 0$ the range is zero, as expected, and it is largest at $\theta = 45^\circ$.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
These are the habits behind the Problem Statement, Solution, and Interpretation sections of the
assignment. For the homework, the problem comes from any technical course they are taking this
semester. The solution must be their own work and follow that course's collaboration policy.
Upload both the PDF and the .tex to Canvas.
:::
